title: 25 Questions to Ask Before Signing a Lease (and Why They Matter)
seo_title: Questions to Ask Before Signing a Lease: 25 to Cover
meta_description: 25 questions to ask before signing a lease: rent, fees, repairs, deposits and breaking the lease, plus what to look for in the answers.
body_html:
A lease is a contract you will live inside for a year or more, so the time to ask questions is before you sign, not after something breaks. The answers protect your budget, your deposit, and your sanity. Bring this list to your tour or send it by email so you have the answers in writing.

Get answers in writing

A friendly leasing agent saying "oh, that's fine" is not the same as a clause in the lease. If an answer matters to you, ask the landlord to put it in the lease or an addendum, or at least confirm it by email. Then read the full lease before signing, including every addendum, and keep a copy.

If you are still deciding when to move, our guide on the best time of year to rent an apartment can help you time your search for better options.

Money: rent, fees, and the deposit

  1. What is the total monthly cost? Ask for rent plus every recurring fee: trash, pest control, amenity, package lockers, technology, parking, pet rent.
  2. What is due at signing? Application fees, admin fees, first month, deposit, pet deposit. Get the exact total.
  3. How much is the security deposit, and what is it used for? Ask whether any portion is non-refundable and how the move-out inspection works.
  4. When is rent due, and what is the grace period? Ask how late fees are calculated.
  5. How can I pay? Online portal, check, money order? Are there fees for paying by card?
  6. How much has rent gone up at renewal in the past? The landlord may not commit to a number, but the answer gives you a sense of what to expect.

Know your deposit rights before you need them. Our guide on how to get your security deposit back walks through it.

Utilities and running costs

  1. Which utilities are included, and which do I set up? Electric, water, sewer, gas, trash, internet.
  2. Is water billed separately or split by a formula? Some buildings divide one water bill among units using a formula rather than individual meters. Ask how it works.
  3. What have average utility bills been for this unit? In hot climates like Texas, summer electric bills can be a real budget item, so it is worth asking.
  4. What internet providers serve the building? Do not assume your preferred provider is available.

Repairs and maintenance

  1. How do I submit a repair request, and how fast do you respond? Look for a written process, like an online portal.
  2. What counts as an emergency, and who do I call after hours? Think no heat, no AC in extreme heat, flooding, gas smell.
  3. Which repairs am I responsible for? Some leases make tenants handle things like air filters, light bulbs, or clogged drains.
  4. Will you need to enter the unit, and how much notice do you give? Entry rules vary by state and lease, so read this clause.
  5. Has the unit had pest, mold, or water issues? Ask directly, and look under sinks and around windows during the tour.

Rules for daily life

  1. What is the pet policy? Breed or weight limits, pet deposits, monthly pet rent.
  2. Can I paint, hang shelves, or mount a TV? Get specifics on wall holes and what you must repair at move-out.
  3. What is the guest policy? Some leases limit how long guests can stay.
  4. Are there quiet hours or noise rules? Useful if you work nights or have kids. If noise worries you, see our guide on how to soundproof an apartment.
  5. How do parking, packages, and trash work? Assigned spots, guest parking, towing rules, package rooms.

Safety and security

  1. Will the locks be rekeyed before I move in? You do not want a previous tenant to still have a working key. In Texas, landlords generally must rekey security devices within a set time after a tenant moves out.
  2. What security features does the unit have? Deadbolts, door viewers, window latches, smoke alarms, lighting in parking areas.
  3. Is renters insurance required, and what coverage minimum? Many landlords require it. Even if yours does not, it is usually worth having.

For more on what to check, read our apartment security tips.

Ending or changing the lease

  1. What happens if I need to break the lease? Ask about early termination fees, reletting fees, and whether you can sublet or find a replacement tenant. Laws also give some tenants specific rights to end a lease early in certain situations, such as military deployment or family violence, so look up the rules for your state.
  2. How much notice do I need to give to move out or renew, and does the lease auto-renew? Some leases convert to month-to-month or renew automatically if you miss a notice deadline. Put that deadline on your calendar the day you sign.

Red flags to watch for

  • Pressure to sign or pay before you have seen the unit or read the lease.
  • Requests to pay by wire transfer, gift card, or cash with no receipt. These are common in rental scams.
  • Blank spaces in the lease that will "be filled in later."
  • Verbal promises the landlord will not put in writing.
  • A unit that does not match the listing, or a "landlord" who cannot show it in person.

Also trust what you see on the tour. Run the faucets, flush the toilet, open and close windows, check under sinks for water stains, and look at the condition of shared hallways and parking areas. How a landlord maintains common spaces is often a good preview of how they will handle your repair requests. Take photos of anything that concerns you and ask about it before signing.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has general consumer resources on avoiding scams and managing housing costs. Lease rules vary by state and city, and this article is not legal advice. If something in your lease confuses you, ask a local tenant organization or legal aid office before signing.

Frequently asked questions

Can I negotiate a lease?

Often, yes. Rent, move-in date, lease length, pet fees, and small upgrades are sometimes negotiable, especially when vacancies are high. The worst answer is no.

Should I sign a lease without seeing the apartment?

Avoid it if you can. If you are moving from far away, ask for a live video tour and verify the landlord or management company is legitimate before sending money.

What should I do before signing?

Read the entire lease, confirm every fee, get promises in writing, and walk the unit to note existing damage. Keep a copy of everything you sign.

Is a verbal agreement binding?

Verbal promises are hard to prove. If it matters, get it in the written lease or an addendum signed by both sides.

What is the one question you wish you had asked before signing? Share it with other renters in the Renting community.
